downgraded.text: Afanasyev reports that, in the opinion of Russian researchers, mavka is the same as navka, a diminutive of nav', that is, "little dead one" (мертвушка).
downgraded.to_text: Afanasyev reports that, in the opinion of "our researchers", mavka is the same as navka, a diminutive of nav', that is, "little dead one" (мертвушка).
downgraded.reason: The page says "нашихъ изслѣдователей" (our researchers); "Russian" is an interpretation the page does not print, so it was narrowed to the page's wording.

flagged.reason: The form is printed letter-spaced as "на вка" on afanasyev1869:p.241, but as the researchers' equivalent of мавка; Afanasyev does not attach навка itself to a people. Ukrainians rests on the neighbouring sentence "Въ Малороссіи и Галиціи" about мавки.

machal1918:p.253 uses Navky as the general term "found throughout the Slavic languages" and lists the Little Russian forms as navk, Nejky, Mavky, Majky; Navky itself is not tied to the Little Russians on the page.

flagged.text: The Mavky are either half-naked or wear only a white shirt.
flagged.reason: Placed in form machal-girls, but on machal1918:p.253 the sentence may describe the Mavky in both their baby and girl appearances; the referent is ambiguous.

flagged.text: For seven years, on Trinity and Whitsun days, the souls of these infants fly through the air begging for baptism; it is thought they can be saved by the words "I baptize thee in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit".

grade_rationale.text: Machal records these beings for the Little Russians (Mavky), for Bulgarians in Macedonia (Navi, Navjaci), for Slovenes (Navje) and for Poles (Latawci).
Afanasyev records mavki in Little-Russia and Galicia, and maiki among the Hutsuls.
Ralston gives Mavki as the Little-Russian and Galician name of the Rusalkas; that passage neither quotes nor cites Afanasyev, so it is counted as independent.
The Ukrainian material therefore rests on three authors (Machal, Afanasyev, Ralston); the Bulgarian, Slovene and Polish rows rest on Machal alone.

Machal's etymology carries a footnote marker whose note is not on the page, so whether his Little Russian passage draws on Afanasyev could not be checked; even counting him once with Afanasyev, two independent authors and four peoples remain.
